idiom_name: a use-prefixed hook returns state + getXProps() functions the call site spreads
implementation_notes: The canonical modern form: a hook owns the state machine (useState/useReducer plus effects) and returns the state together with prop getters - functions that return the props for one element, composing the consumer's own handlers and ids instead of overwriting them (the callAll trick from Kent C. Dodds' prop-getters article). Downshift's documentation describes its hooks as providing 'the stateful logic needed to make the corresponding component functional and accessible', which is exactly the behaviour half; the call site supplies every element and spreads the getters. Keep the classic render-prop component when the behaviour must own a component boundary, and keep the state machine framework-free when the same behaviour must run in other frameworks.
pitfalls: Hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level of a component or another hook, or the call-order state mapping is displaced.
Returned callbacks capture the render's values; without stable identities or refs, handlers keep stale state and effects re-subscribe on every render.
Spreading a getter before your own props (or after, without handler composition) either drops the primitive's handler or the consumer's - the merge order is part of the contract.
Generated ids must be stable across server and client renders (useId rather than a counter), or aria-* attributes mismatch after hydration.

variants.name: Render-prop (renderless) component
variants.implementation_notes: The original form: the component owns the behaviour and calls the function the consumer passed - as the legacy React documentation puts it, 'a component with a render prop takes a function that returns a React element and calls it instead of implementing its own render logic', and any function-valued prop counts. Downshift's component form still ships this shape. Choose it when the behaviour must live in a component (class or function) that the consumer nests in its tree; the same documentation notes that for many cases render props have been replaced by custom hooks, so prefer the hook dialect in new React code and reserve this form for libraries that must also serve non-hook frameworks.
pitfalls: The function child must return a React element; returning a plain string or array of elements confuses consumers and the propTypes contract.
Each render creates a new function value, so memoization around the component is defeated unless the child is stable or the component accepts a memoized tree.
Inline render functions hide pull-based work: consumers often re-run expensive logic inside the render callback because the component offers no hook to memoize it.

variants.name: Framework-agnostic headless state machine (Zag-style)
variants.idiom_name: createMachine + per-framework connect() exposing state/prop getters
variants.implementation_notes: The behaviour is modelled once as a state machine and consumed through thin framework adapters: Zag describes itself as 'a framework agnostic toolkit for implementing complex, interactive, and accessible UI components', powered by state machines, whose machine APIs are 'completely unstyled' and leave the styling solution to the consumer, with adapters for React, Solid and Vue. The machine's output is a connect/getters surface per framework, so the markup half stays ordinary framework code and the behaviour ports by adapter only. Choose this when the same interaction must exist in several frameworks, and accept the extra dependency and indirection when it does not.
pitfalls: A machine that is not serializable (callbacks, class instances in context) cannot be persisted or rehydrated, which removes one of the main reasons to use a machine.
Adapters leak framework specifics (refs, event objects) unless the machine only consumes plain events - put DOM concerns in the adapter, not in the machine.
Two adapters for the same machine can drift if shared behaviour is duplicated in the adapter layer; keep all transitions in the machine.
